summary.text: For \(K=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}193\), the residue classes of every exponent modulo \(48\) are covered by congruence conditions forcing one of \(3,5,7,17,97,673,257\) to divide \(K2^e+1\); since \(K\) is odd and greater than one, this proves that \(K\) is a Sierpiński number. At \(n=5{,}319{,}426\), \(a(n)=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}189\), so \(K=a(n)+4\) lies strictly between \(a(n)\) and \(a(n)+28\), disproving their consecutiveness.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=9{,}454{,}129+11{,}184{,}810n.
\]
Recall that a positive integer \(k\) is a Sierpiński number here if it is odd, greater than \(1\), and, for every positive integer \(e\), the number
\[
k2^e+1
\]
is not prime.

We disprove the assertion by considering the index
\[
n_0=5{,}319{,}426
\]
and the integer
\[
K=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}193.
\]
We will first prove that \(K\) is a Sierpiński number, and then show that it lies strictly between \(a(n_0)\) and \(a(n_0)+28\).

## 1. A covering system for the exponents

For every integer \(e\), at least one of the following seven congruences holds:
\[
\begin{aligned}
e&\equiv0\pmod 2,\\
e&\equiv3\pmod 4,\\
e&\equiv1\pmod 3,\\
e&\equiv1\pmod 8,\\
e&\equiv5\pmod {48},\\
e&\equiv21\pmod {48},\\
e&\equiv13\pmod {16}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]
Here is a direct proof that these classes cover all integers. If \(e\) is even, the first congruence applies. Suppose, therefore, that \(e\) is odd. If \(e\equiv3\pmod4\), the second congruence applies. We may thus suppose that \(e\equiv1\pmod4\). If \(e\equiv1\pmod3\), the third class applies. Otherwise, combining \(e\equiv1\pmod4\) with \(e\not\equiv1\pmod3\) shows that
\[
e\equiv5\quad\hbox{or}\quad9\pmod {12}.
\]
Equivalently, modulo \(24\), the remaining possibilities are
\[
e\equiv5,9,17,21\pmod {24}.
\]
The residues \(9\) and \(17\) modulo \(24\) are both congruent to \(1\pmod8\), so they are covered by the fourth class. We are left with
\[
e\equiv5\quad\hbox{or}\quad21\pmod {24}.
\]
Modulo \(48\), these possibilities split into
\[
5,29,21,45.
\]
The residues \(5\) and \(21\) are respectively the fifth and sixth classes in (1), while both \(29\) and \(45\) are congruent to \(13\pmod {16}\). This proves the claimed covering.

## 2. Divisors associated with the covering classes

To the seven classes in (1), associate respectively the primes
\[
3,\ 5,\ 7,\ 17,\ 97,\ 673,\ 257.
\]
For each pair, we will prove that the associated prime divides \(K2^e+1\) whenever \(e\) is in the relevant class.

The needed residue of \(K\) modulo each of these primes is as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr}
p&3&5&7&17&97&673&257\\ \hline
K\bmod p&2&3&3&8&3&8&249.
\end{array}
\tag{2}
\]
For completeness, these residues follow from the exact divisions
\[
\begin{aligned}
K&=3(19{,}832{,}259{,}524{,}397)+2,\\
K&=5(11{,}899{,}355{,}714{,}638)+3,\\
K&=7(8{,}499{,}539{,}796{,}170)+3,\\
K&=17(3{,}499{,}810{,}504{,}305)+8,\\
K&=97(613{,}368{,}851{,}270)+3,\\
K&=673(88{,}405{,}317{,}345)+8,\\
K&=257(231{,}504{,}974{,}992)+249.
\end{aligned}
\]

We now treat all seven exponent classes.

### Case 1: \(e\equiv0\pmod2\)

Modulo \(3\), we have \(2^2\equiv1\). Hence an even exponent satisfies \(2^e\equiv1\pmod3\). By (2), \(K\equiv2\pmod3\), and therefore
\[
K2^e+1\equiv2\cdot1+1\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
Thus \(3\mid K2^e+1\).

### Case 2: \(e\equiv3\pmod4\)

Modulo \(5\), \(2^4\equiv1\), so \(2^e\equiv2^3\equiv3\pmod5\). Since \(K\equiv3\pmod5\),
\[
K2^e+1\equiv3\cdot3+1=10\equiv0\pmod5.
\]
Thus \(5\mid K2^e+1\).

### Case 3: \(e\equiv1\pmod3\)

Modulo \(7\), \(2^3=8\equiv1\). Hence \(2^e\equiv2\pmod7\). Since \(K\equiv3\pmod7\),
\[
K2^e+1\equiv3\cdot2+1=7\equiv0\pmod7.
\]
Thus \(7\mid K2^e+1\).

### Case 4: \(e\equiv1\pmod8\)

Modulo \(17\), \(2^8=256\equiv1\). Thus \(2^e\equiv2\pmod {17}\). Since \(K\equiv8\pmod {17}\),
\[
K2^e+1\equiv8\cdot2+1=17\equiv0\pmod {17}.
\]
Thus \(17\mid K2^e+1\).

### Case 5: \(e\equiv5\pmod {48}\)

We first check the period modulo \(97\). We have
\[
2^8=256\equiv62\pmod {97},
\]
and hence
\[
2^{16}\equiv62^2=3844\equiv61\pmod {97}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{24}=2^{16}2^8\equiv61\cdot62=3782\equiv-1\pmod {97},
\]
because \(3783=39\cdot97\). Squaring gives
\[
2^{48}\equiv1\pmod {97}.
\]
Therefore, when \(e\equiv5\pmod {48}\),
\[
2^e\equiv2^5=32\pmod {97}.
\]
Using \(K\equiv3\pmod {97}\), we obtain
\[
K2^e+1\equiv3\cdot32+1=97\equiv0\pmod {97}.
\]
Thus \(97\mid K2^e+1\).

### Case 6: \(e\equiv21\pmod {48}\)

We similarly compute modulo \(673\). First,
\[
2^{10}=1024\equiv351\pmod {673}.
\]
Squaring gives
\[
2^{20}\equiv351^2=123201\equiv42\pmod {673},
\]
since \(123201=183\cdot673+42\). Hence
\[
2^{21}\equiv84\pmod {673}.
\]
It follows that
\[
2^{24}=2^{21}2^3\equiv84\cdot8=672\equiv-1\pmod {673},
\]
and consequently
\[
2^{48}\equiv1\pmod {673}.
\]
If \(e\equiv21\pmod {48}\), then \(2^e\equiv84\pmod {673}\). Since \(K\equiv8\pmod {673}\),
\[
K2^e+1\equiv8\cdot84+1=673\equiv0\pmod {673}.
\]
Thus \(673\mid K2^e+1\).

### Case 7: \(e\equiv13\pmod {16}\)

Modulo \(257\),
\[
2^8=256\equiv-1\pmod {257},
\]
so \(2^{16}\equiv1\pmod {257}\). Moreover,
\[
2^{13}=2^8 2^5\equiv(-1)\cdot32\equiv225\pmod {257}.
\]
Thus, if \(e\equiv13\pmod {16}\), then \(2^e\equiv225\pmod {257}\). Also \(K\equiv249\equiv-8\pmod {257}\), and hence
\[
K2^e+1\equiv(-8)\cdot225+1=-1799=-7\cdot257\equiv0\pmod {257}.
\]
Thus \(257\mid K2^e+1\).

## 3. The integer \(K\) is a Sierpiński number

The integer
\[
K=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}193
\]
is odd and is greater than \(1\). Let \(e>0\) be arbitrary. By the covering argument in Section 1, \(e\) belongs to at least one of the seven classes in (1). The corresponding argument in Section 2 supplies a divisor
\[
p\in\{3,5,7,17,97,673,257\}
\]
of \(K2^e+1\).

Every such \(p\) is at least \(2\), and each is much smaller than \(K\). Since \(e>0\), in particular
\[
p<K<K2^e+1.
\]
Thus \(p\) is a nontrivial proper divisor of \(K2^e+1\). It follows that \(K2^e+1\) is not prime. This holds for every positive exponent \(e\), so \(K\) is a Sierpiński number.

## 4. \(K\) lies strictly between the proposed consecutive terms

At the chosen index \(n_0=5{,}319{,}426\), direct arithmetic gives
\[
11{,}184{,}810\cdot5{,}319{,}426
=59{,}496{,}769{,}119{,}060.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n_0)
&=9{,}454{,}129+59{,}496{,}769{,}119{,}060\\
&=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}189.
\end{aligned}
\]
Comparing this with \(K\), we have
\[
K=a(n_0)+4.
\]
Consequently,
\[
a(n_0)<K<a(n_0)+28;
\]
indeed, the two gaps are respectively \(4\) and \(24\):
\[
a(n_0)+28=59{,}496{,}778{,}573{,}217=K+24.
\]

We have therefore exhibited a Sierpiński number \(K\) strictly between \(a(5{,}319{,}426)\) and \(a(5{,}319{,}426)+28\). Hence those two endpoint integers cannot be consecutive Sierpiński numbers. Since the conjecture claimed this consecutiveness for every \(n\ge0\), this single index disproves the conjecture.
